# Spherically Symmetric Potentials

We will consider the motion of a particle in a central force field. We will
consider the Coulomb field experienced by an electron in a hydrogenic atom and
a three dimensional harmonic oscillator.

## The general solution
For a potential function of the form
$$
V(\bv{r}) = V(r),
$$ {#eq-spp1}
and the hamiltonian is
$$
-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\left[\frac{1}{r^2}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r^2
\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\right) + \frac{1}{r^2\sin\theta}\frac{\partial}
{\partial\theta}\left(\sin\theta\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\right) +
\frac{1}{r^2\sin^2\theta}\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\phi^2}\right]+ V(r).
$$ {#eq-spp2}
The Schr&ouml;odinger equation can be solved using the standard separation of
variables method by writing
$$
\psi(r, \theta, \phi) = R(r)\Theta(\theta)\Phi(\phi)
$$ {#eq-spp3}
so that 
$$
\begin{split}
\frac{\Theta\Phi}{r^2}\frac{d}{dr}\left(r^2\frac{dR}{dr}\right) +
\frac{R\Phi}{r^2\sin\theta}\frac{d}{d\theta}\left(\sin\theta\frac{d\Theta}
{d\theta}\right) + \\
\frac{R\Theta}{r^2\sin^2\theta}\frac{d^2\Phi}{d\phi^2} +
\frac{2m}{\hbar^2}(E - V(r))\psi = 0.
\end{split}
$$ {#eq-spp4}
Multiplying both sides by $r^2\sin^2\theta/\psi$,
$$
\begin{split}
\frac{\sin^2\theta}{R}\frac{d}{dr}\left(r^2\frac{dR}{dr}\right) +
\frac{\sin\theta}{\Phi}\frac{d}{d\theta}\left(\sin\theta\frac{d\Theta}
{d\theta}\right) + \\
\frac{2mr^2\sin^2\theta}{\hbar^2}(E - V(r)) = 
- \frac{1}{\Phi}\frac{d^2\Phi}{d\phi^2}.
\end{split}
$$ {#eq-spp5}
Since the lhs depends only on $r$ and $\theta$ while the rhs only on $\phi$, 
the above equation can be true only if each side is a constant. We call it
$m_l^2$. The rhs, therefore, gives
$$
\frac{d^2\Phi}{d\phi^2} = -m_l^2\Phi,
$$ {#eq-spp6}
whose solution is
$$
\Phi(\phi) = \alpha_1 e^{im_l\phi} + \alpha_2 e^{-im_l\phi},
$$ {#eq-spp7}
where $\alpha_1$ and $\alpha_2$ are constants of integration. Since $\Phi(\phi
 + 2\pi)$ must be equal to $\Phi(\phi)$, the constant $m_l$ must be an integer.
Additionally, we also require that $\Phi(\phi) = \Phi(-\phi)$ so that the
two constants of integrations must be equal. That is, $\Phi(\phi) = \alpha_1
(e^{im_l\phi} + e^{-im_l\phi})$. Since $m_l$ can be any integer, positive or 
negative, we can as well write $\Phi(\phi) = 2\alpha_1 e^{im_l\phi}$. The 
normalisation condition
$$
\int_0^{2\pi}|\Phi|^2d\phi = 1
$$
gives
$$
\Phi(\phi) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{im_l\phi}.
$$ {#eq-spp8}
The lhs of @eq-spp4 too can be separated into
$$
\begin{eqnarray*}
-\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\frac{d}{d\theta}\left(\sin\theta\frac{d\Theta}{d\theta}
\right) + \frac{m_l^2}{\sin^2\theta} = \beta \\
\frac{1}{R}\frac{d}{dr}\left(r^2\frac{dR}{dr}\right) + \frac{2mr^2}{\hbar^2}
\left(E - V(r)\right) = \beta,
\end{eqnarray*}
$$ {#eq-spp9}
where $\beta$ is a constant of separation. We now consider the $\theta$ 
equation. To solve it, we use the transformation $x = \cos\theta$ to get
$$
(1 - x^2)\Theta^\tp - 2x\Theta^\op + \left(\beta - \frac{m_l^2}{1-x^2}\right)
\Theta = 0.
$$ {#eq-spp10}
The coefficient of the terms of this equation blow up at $x = \pm 1$. Therefore,
applying the Frobenius method needs precautions. At a singularity like $x = 1$,
$1 - x^2 \approx 2(1 - x)$ and $2x \approx 2$. The term $-m_l^2/(1 - x^2)$ 
dominates over $\beta$ to a great extent so that we can as well ignore $\beta$.
Therefore, @eq-spp10 becomes
$$
2(1-x)\Theta^\tp - 2\Theta^\op  - \frac{m_l^2}{2(1-x)}\Theta = 0.
$$ {#eq-spp11}
We consider a trial solution of the form $\Theta(x) = (1 - x)^a$ so that the
above equation gives $a = \pm m_l/2$. To prevent the function from blowing up
near $x = 1$, we choose $a = |m_l|/2$. A similar analysis at the pole $x = -1$ 
gives $\Theta(x) \approx (1 + x)^{|m_l|/2}$ so that we can write the general 
$\Theta(x)$ as
$$
\Theta(x) = (1 - x^2)^{|m_l|/2}P(x).
$$ {#eq-spp12}
We compute its first two derivaties as
$$
\begin{eqnarray*}
\Theta^\op(x) &=& (1 - x^2)^{|m_l|/2 - 1}\left(-|m_l|xP+(1-x^2)P^\op\right) \\
\Theta^\tp(x) &=& (1 - x^2)^{|m_l|/2 - 2}
\left[(1-x^2)^2P^\tp - 2|m_l|x(1-x^2)P^\op \right.\\
 & & \left.- |m_l|(1-x^2)P + |m_l|(|m_l|-2) x^2P(x)\right]
\end{eqnarray*}
$$ {#eq-spp13}
Substituting these expressions in @eq-spp10} gives
$$
(1 - x^2)P^\tp - 2(|m_l| + 1)xP^\op + (\beta - |m_l|(|m_l| + 1))P = 0.
$$ {#eq-spp14}
We now use the series solution
$$
P(x) = \sum_{k = 0}^\infty c_k x^k
$$ {#eq-spp15}
to get the recurrence relation
$$
c_{k+2} = \frac{k^2 + 2|m_l|k + |m_l|^2 + |m_l| + k - \beta}{(k+1)(k+2)}.
$$ {#eq-spp16}
It will terminate only if
$$ 
\beta = (k + |m_l|)^2 + (k + |m_l|) = (k + |m_l| + 1)(k + |m_l|)
$$ {#eq-spp17}
Since $k$ and $m_l$ are both integers, $\beta$ is of the form
$$
\beta = l(l + 1), l \in \mathbb{Z}.
$$ {#eq-spp18}
Equation @eq-spp14 now becomes
$$
(1 - x^2)P^\tp - 2(|m_l| + 1)xP^\op + (l(l+1) - |m_l|(|m_l| + 1))P = 0.
$$ {#eq-spp19}
This equation is closely related to the Legendre equation
$$
(1 - x^2)P_l^\tp - 2(|m_l| + 1)xP_l^\op + l(l+1)P_l = 0
$$ {#eq-spp20}
where $P_l$ is the Legendre polynomial of order $l$. If we differentiate this
equation $|m_l$ times, we get
$$
(1 - x^2)P^{(|m_l| + 2)} - 2(|m_l| + 1)xP^{(|m_l| + 1)} + 
(l(l+1) - |m_l|(|m_l| + 1))P^{(|m_l|)} = 0.
$$ {#eq-spp21}
Comparing this with equation @eq-spp19 we see that its solution can be 
written as 
$$
P_l^{|m_l|}(x) = \frac{d^{|m_l|}}{dx^{|m_l|}} P_l(x).
$$ {#eq-spp22}
It is called the associated Legendre polynomial. It satisfies the relation
$$
\int_{-1}^1 P_l^{|m_l|}(x)P_k^{|m_l|}(x) = \frac{2}{2l+1}
\frac{(l + |m_l|)!}{(l - |m_l|)!}\delta_{lk}
$$ {#eq-spp23}
so that the normalised solution to the $\theta$ equation is
$$
\Theta(\theta) = \sqrt{\frac{2l+1}{2}\frac{(l-|m_l|)!}{(l+|m_l|)!}}
\sin^{|m_l|}(\theta)P_l^{|m_l|}(\cos\theta).
$$ {#eq-spp24}
The combination,
$$
\Theta(\theta)\Phi(\phi) = \sqrt{\frac{2l+1}{2}\frac{(l-|m_l|)!}{(l+|m_l|)!}}
\frac{\sin^{|m_l|}(\theta)}{\sqrt{2\pi}}P_l^{|m_l|}(\cos\theta) e^{i|m_l|\phi}
$$ {#eq-spp25}
is called a spherical harmonic and is denoted by $Y_{l, m_l}(\theta, \phi)$.
